extraction.name: SeamlessAlign
extraction.description: SeamlessAlign is the largest open dataset for multimodal translation, totaling 470,000 hours of automatically aligned speech translations. It covers 37 languages and includes English speech paired with non-English text, non-English speech paired with English text, and non-English speech paired with English speech, created through parallel data mining using SONAR embeddings.
extraction.creator: Seamless Communication (Meta AI)
extraction.citeAs: Seamless Communication et al., SeamlessM4T: Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation, arXiv:2308.11596, 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was assembled through multiple collection strategies: (1) 4 million hours of raw audio were obtained from a publicly available repository of crawled web data; (2) text data was drawn entirely from the NLLB dataset, using the same data sources as that project; (3) human-labeled ASR transcriptions were collected for at least 100 hours per language for most of the 37 supported languages; (4) speech-to-text and speech-to-speech aligned pairs were created via automated parallel data mining using SONAR embeddings over the collected audio and text corpora; (5) pseudo-labeled data was generated by applying NLLB-200-3.3B to ASR transcriptions; (6) existing open-source and licensed S2TT and ASR datasets were incorporated as primary supervised data.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping; Secondary Data analysis; Manual Human Curator; Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some samples from the CVSS evaluation data were missing in 8 out of 21 languages: Catalan, German, Estonian, French, Italian, Mongolian, Persian, and Portuguese. For Maltese, only a small amount of raw audio was available. Several languages had zero raw audio for mining (e.g., Asturian, Cebuano, West Central Oromo, Kamba, Kabuverdianu, Luxembourgish, Luo, Maithili, Meitei, Occitan, Shona, Sindhi, Xhosa). Some language directions were left unmined (indicated by dashes in Table 10).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw audio: 4 million hours from a publicly available repository of crawled web data (approximately 1 million hours in English). Text data: the NLLB parallel text dataset covering 200 languages. Human-labeled ASR transcriptions collected for 37 languages (totaling approximately 43,772 hours). Existing open-source corpora including VoxLingua107, FLEURS, CoVoST 2, MuST-C, EuroParl-ST, VoxPopuli, CVSS, and others used for supervised training data. Test data for LID model drawn from FLEURS test set, VoxLingua107 development set, VAANI, IIITH, and KENCORPUS.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human evaluators assessed translation quality using the XSTS protocol (semantic meaning preservation) and MOS protocol (naturalness, sound quality, clarity of speech). For XSTS, annotators examined source-target audio or audio-text pairs and rated semantic similarity. Prior to annotating, all annotators completed monolingual English practice evaluations with score justifications. In cases where 3 annotators disagreed by 2 or more score values, 2 additional annotators evaluated the same item, bringing the total to 5. A cross-lingual calibration set was included to reduce annotator bias. For MOS, annotators rated clarity, sound quality, and naturalness on a 1-5 Likert scale. Human error analysis of toxicity detection outputs was also performed by team members to determine true positives vs. false positives.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For XSTS, the median score over annotators per audio pair was taken as the final score; language-level scores were calibrated using the mean score on the calibration set via 'moderated calibration' methodology. For MOS, the median of annotator scores was collected per item. Calibration was not performed for MOS. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate language score uncertainty.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 (with up to 5 for items where annotators disagreed by 2 or more score values; some MOS language directions had only 1 annotator per item)
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: ETOX (word-list-based toxicity detection using Toxicity-200 word lists); Whisper-Medium and Whisper-Large-v2 (ASR models used for ASR-BLEU and ASR-ETOX); NLLB-200-3.3B (used for pseudo-labeling ASR data with T2TT); MMS-TTS (used to synthesize speech from Multilingual HolisticBias text for bias evaluation); fairseq S^2 default 'en' transformer-tts model (used to extend HolisticBias to speech); Blaser 2.0 (automatic model-based quality estimation metric)
extraction.rai:dataBiases: SeamlessM4T overgeneralizes to masculine forms when translating from neutral terms (with an average preference of ~10%); model shows a lack of robustness when varying gender by an amount of ~3%; masculine representation is predominant in most of the analyzed datasets (EuroParl, Flores, Fleurs, CoVoST 2, LibriSpeech, MultilingualLibriSpeech, and mined SeamlessAlign data); unequal training datasets can lead to demographic and representational biases
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: SeamlessM4T is a research model and is not released for production deployment; trained on general domain data and not intended for domain-specific inputs such as medical or legal domains; not intended for long-form translation as the model was trained on short text and speech inputs; SeamlessM4T translations cannot be used as certified translations; ASR performance may vary based on gender, race, accent, or language; performance when translating slang or proper nouns may be inconsistent across high and low-resource languages; word list-based toxicity detection (ETOX) tends to over-detect terms only toxic in specific contexts and relies on precise tokenization; noun list-based gender imbalance detection shares limitations of word list-based techniques; Fleurs test set is limited in speaker diversity (maximum of 3 speakers); mining currently focused on 37 of the 100 target languages
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: SeamlessM4T could augment world-readiness by lowering barriers in cross-lingual communication, particularly benefiting those with accessibility needs (e.g., people who are blind or with visual impairment, those lacking reading or writing skills), and speakers of languages with script variance or multiple writing systems; however, access could make groups with lower levels of digital literacy more vulnerable to misinformation or online scams if bad actors misappropriate the work; toxic, biased, or false outputs could adversely impact those who rely on translations for important decisions, particularly related to health and safety; the authors urge that SeamlessM4T-fueled applications be viewed as an augmentation device rather than a replacement for language learning or reliable human interpreters, especially in high-stakes legal or medical situations
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The training data used for model development were mined from various publicly available sources on the web; although heavily cleaned, personally identifiable information may not be entirely eliminated
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) for 96 languages; speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) from 100 source speech languages into 35 target speech languages; speech-to-text translation (S2TT) from 100 source speech languages into 95 target text languages; text-to-speech translation (T2ST) from 95 source text languages into 35 target speech languages; text-to-text translation (T2TT) from 95 source text languages into 95 target text languages; text-to-speech synthesis (TTS) for 36 languages; primary intended users are researchers and the machine translation research community; information on finetuning recipes is provided in the seamless_communication repository
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Pseudo-labeling was used to generate S2TT labels for ASR data using NLLB-200-3.3B. Pseudo-labeling with text-to-unit (T2U) models was used to convert text into discrete acoustic units for S2ST training. Mined data from SeamlessAlign was added to training sets (up to 400 hours per direction for S2TT, up to 2,500 hours per direction for S2ST) based on Sonar alignment scores. The HolisticBias dataset was extended to speech by applying a TTS model (fairseq S^2 transformer-tts) to generate synthesized speech. The Multilingual HolisticBias dataset was extended to speech using the MMS-TTS model.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For text data, the same data sources, cleaning, and filtering steps from NLLB were used. For audio data: URLs were deduplicated, audio files were downloaded and resampled at 16KHz, non-speech data was filtered using an audio event detection (AED) model, and Voice Activity Detection (VAD) was applied for segmentation followed by over-segmentation. LID filtering was applied by estimating Gaussian distributions of LID scores and rejecting approximately 8% of data below a per-language threshold. For human-labeled S2TT data: special tokens such as <silence> and <no-speech> were removed, length filtering removed examples exceeding 100 sub-word tokens or with text-to-audio length ratio exceeding 5 sub-words per second, and utterances shorter than 0.1 seconds or longer than 50 seconds were removed. A toxicity filter removed pairs with toxicity imbalance (difference in toxic items between source and target above a threshold of 1). Pairs with text longer than 250 sub-words, more than 20% emojis, more than 50% punctuations, or more than 50% spaces were removed. For S2ST pseudo-labeled data, pairs with audio-per-text-token ratio exceeding 0.5 seconds per token were filtered. The SentencePiece tokenizer vocabulary was retrained at 256K size on NLLB data with forced inclusion of top Chinese and Japanese characters appearing at least 15 times in training data. For Blaser 2.0 training data, audio longer than 30 seconds was filtered out. For the bias evaluation, numerical numbers in sentences were manually converted to words before TTS processing.
